Basics of beer brewing

Ingredients of beer: water, malt, hops, yeast. The brewing process: mashing, boiling, fermentation, conditioning.

Base maltsPilsner malt · Pale ale malt · Vienna malt
Specialty maltsRoasted malts · Caramel malts
Other maltsWheat malt · Rye malt
Aroma hopsCitra, Simcoe, Mosaic (American) · Saaz, Hallertau (European noble) · Nelson Sauvin, Motueka (New Zealand)
Dual-purpose hopsCascade · Centennial
Bittering hopsMagnum, Columbus (high alpha acid) · Northern Brewer, Perle (moderate alpha acid)
Water sourceSpring water · City water · Well water · Distilled/RO water
AdjustmentsGypsum · Epsom salt · Calcium chloride · Table salt · Baking soda · Acid
What yeast produces
  • Alcohol
  • Carbon dioxide
  • Flavor compounds: esters, phenols, higher alcohols (the unique taste and aroma of different beer styles)
  • Other byproducts: glycerol · diacetyl (off-flavor if not managed) · sulfur compounds (off-flavor if not managed)

The brewing process

Module 2 · 13:25

Why we do QC

Same recipe → same beer, every batch

Product quality

  • The beer meets its specification
  • No defects, safe to drink

Product consistency

  • Batch 1 and batch 100 taste the same
  • Example: target FG 1.015, every batch, within an agreed tolerance

Customers come back for the beer they remember.

Types of QC analysis

Measurable · comparable · repeatable, just like any lab science.

What we look atMalt appearance, foreign matter, color, clarity/haze
Unit / toolEBC/SRM color, haze, sieve test
At 12 PlatoBrix (refractometer)
What we look atAlcohol, sweetness/extract, bitterness, pH
Unit / tool% ABV, °Plato / Brix / SG, IBU, pH meter
At 12 PlatoOG, pH
What we look atYeast count & viability, yeast strain, contaminating microbes
Unit / toolcells/mL (microscope), plating, PCR
At 12 PlatoYeast health by sensory and fermentation performance

The limit of numbers

  • Flavor = hundreds of compounds working together
  • Measuring everything takes too much time and money
  • Some compounds matter at ng/L, below what basic lab tools can detect

Sensory at 12 Plato

  • Trained tasters = a calibrated instrument
  • Every batch: “Does it match the target? Yes / No / Why?”
  • Fast, low-cost, and judged the way our customers judge

Lab numbers tell us what changed; sensory tells us whether it matters.

Mash enzyme explorer

Drag the mash temperature and see which enzymes are in their working range.

65°C(149 °F)
35506580 °C
EnzymeActionOptimum °CpHMain result
  • β-amylase (exo-acting) trims maltose from the non-reducing ends of starch chains but cannot pass α-1,6 branch points.
  • α-amylase (endo-acting) cuts α-1,4 bonds inside the chains, producing dextrins of varying length and new chain ends for β-amylase.

Typical ranges; actual activity depends on malt, mash thickness and time. Sources: AHA; Kunze, Technology Brewing & Malting.

Measuring equipment used in brewing

Module 2 · continued

Fermentation QC

Fermentation timeline · schematic, not to scale · D = day
1. Temperature control
What to monitor
  • Tank temperature vs. style setpoint
  • Probe calibration against a reference thermometer
  • Glycol / jacket performance
  • No large temperature swings
Why it matters
  • Fermentation is exothermic: active beer runs warmer than the setpoint
  • Too warm → more esters and fusel alcohols
  • Plan free-rise and the diacetyl rest near the end
2. Gravity monitoring
How to measure
  • Hydrometer: correct for sample temperature
  • Refractometer: needs alcohol correction once fermentation starts
  • Record the gravity drop daily
  • FG = same reading on 2–3 consecutive days
Use the numbers
  • Apparent attenuation = (OG − FG) ÷ OG, in °Plato (try the calculator)
  • Compare with the yeast's expected attenuation
  • A forced fermentation test shows the attainable limit
3. Yeast health
What to check
  • Pitch rate (cells/mL/°P)
  • Viability: live/dead staining
  • Vitality: how active the cells are
  • Oxygen at pitching
  • Slurry age, color and smell
Rules of thumb
  • Ale ≈ 0.75 million cells/mL/°P
  • Lager ≈ 1.5 million cells/mL/°P
  • Krausen and bubbling are only supporting signs
4. Fermentation timeline
Phases
  • Lag: yeast adapts and takes up O₂
  • Exponential: fast growth, high krausen
  • Stationary: sugar runs out
  • Conditioning: reabsorbs diacetyl and acetaldehyde, flocculates
Warning signs
  • Long lag → low pitch, low O₂, cold wort or weak yeast
  • Stuck/sluggish → check temperature, nutrients, yeast health
5. Sensory checkpoints
During fermentation
  • Sample daily from the sample valve
  • Early: sulfur (H₂S) and green apple are normal
  • Late: check for diacetyl before cooling
  • Appearance: haze, color, yeast in suspension
VDK forced test
  • Heat a sample to ~60–70 °C for 10–20 min
  • Cool it, then smell against an unheated sample
  • Buttery only in the heated sample → precursor remains → do not crash yet
6. Documentation
What to record
  • Brew log: OG, temperatures, pitch, gravity, pH
  • Batch tracking: ingredient lots, yeast generation
  • Deviations and corrective actions
Turn records into control
  • Plot FG, pH and days-to-FG across batches
  • Control charts show drift before it becomes a defect
  • Data makes troubleshooting faster
Module 3 · 14:15

Sensory analysis

The sensory process in brewing is a critical step used to evaluate and ensure the quality and consistency of the beer through human senses.

Flavor = taste + aroma (orthonasal & retronasal) + trigeminal sensations

Beer attributes to evaluate

In BJCP order. Tap each to open.

True or false?Each part of the tongue tastes only one flavorTap to reveal
Myth alertFalseEvery area with taste buds detects all five basic tastes (Chandrashekar et al., 2006, Nature).

Retronasal olfaction

  • Warming in the mouth
  • Mixing with saliva (enzymes)
  • Chewing and swallowing movements
  • CO₂ release carries volatiles
  • Tip: swallow, then exhale through the nose

Threshold types

Measured with ascending forced-choice tests (ASTM E679); thresholds vary widely between tasters.

Module 4 · 15:20

Sanitation, draught QC & safety

Cleaning cycle

  1. Pre-rinse
  2. Caustic wash
  3. Intermediate rinse
  4. Final rinse
  5. Sanitizing rinse
OptionalAcid wash (54–60 °C): dissolves mineral scale (beerstone) and protein residues, helps passivate stainless steel and neutralizes residual caustic. Air blow: remove remaining moisture.

Residue testing in a microbrewery

Final rinse waterCollect samples of the final rinse water from tanks and pipes for testing.
Swab testUse swabs to check the surfaces of cleaned tanks or pipes for residues.
Conductivity meterMeasure the conductivity of the final rinse water to detect residual chemicals.
pH strips or pH meterCheck the final rinse water pH is in the normal range, showing no residual acids or bases.
Draught QC: keeping the lines clean
  • Every 2 weeks: clean beer lines with a caustic line cleaner
  • Recirculate: caustic solution through the full line, then rinse until the rinse water matches tap water (pH/conductivity)
  • Quarterly: acid clean to remove beerstone; fully disassemble FOBs
  • Every cleaning: take apart and brush faucets and couplers
  • Why: biofilm in lines causes sour, buttery (diacetyl) and hazy beer at the tap
  • Safety: goggles and chemical gloves; never let cleaner reach a customer
Draught QC: temperature, gas and glassware
  • Temperature: store and serve at 1–3 °C (34–38 °F); warm beer foams
  • Carbonation: most beers 2.2–2.8 volumes CO₂
  • Gas pressure: balance applied pressure against total line resistance
  • Long-draw systems: use a CO₂/N₂ blend (e.g., 70/30) to avoid over-carbonation
  • Foam or flat beer: check temperature first, then pressure, then line length
  • “Beer-clean” glass: sheeting, salt and lacing tests

Safety: CO₂ is invisible

Colorless, odorless and heavier than air; it collects in tanks, cellars and pits. Drag to see the limits.

5,000ppm CO₂(0.5%)
  • Monitor: fixed CO₂ alarms in cold rooms, keg stores and near fermenters
  • Confined space: never enter a tank without ventilation, gas testing, a permit and a standby person
  • Rescue: untrained rescuers often become victims too; do not enter, call for help

Safety: chemicals, pressure and heat

  • Chemicals: goggles or face shield, chemical gloves, apron; eyewash station nearby
  • Mixing: add chemical to water, never water to chemical; never mix chlorine with acid
  • Caustic + CO₂: purge CO₂ before caustic cleaning; vacuum can collapse a tank
  • Pressure: never exceed the vessel rating; check relief valves; depressurize before opening
  • Gas cylinders: secured upright and chained
  • Heat and machines: hot wort and steam; lock out pumps and mixers before maintenance
